strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework: HSR Bellman operator is properly derived with formal proof that it is a contraction mapping (Theorem 3.1), ensuring convergence guarantees for online learning

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: Multiple grid-world topologies tested (4-room, augmented 4-room, loop, corridor; Figure S3) with proper statistical testing (two-sided t-tests, p-values, df reported), 20 random seeds, and controlled experimental setup with consistent hyperparameters

Multiple demonstrated benefits: Significant transfer efficiency gains (p=0.008), superior NMF basis performance (p<1e-16 vs. baselines), robust exploration scaling (Figure 6c), and benefits persist with online-constructed options (Figure S6)
Strong interpretability results: Discovered NMF factors naturally align with bottleneck states (Figure 4e), bridging learned representations with meaningful topological structure for navigation tasks

Thorough ablations and robustness checks: Transfer gains consistent across different topologies (Figure S3), option types (Figure S4b: eigenoptions, covering, random), and option budgets; online option construction validated

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear exposition with informative visualizations (especially Figure 1 pipeline), comprehensive implementation details (Appendix C), promised code release, and detailed algorithms

Key insight on NMF amenability: The observation that HSR's piecewise-smooth structure is amenable to NMF (vs. feature collapse in standard SR) is novel and practically useful for sparse representation discovery
weaknesses: Severe experimental scope limitation: All experiments confined to discrete, tabular grid-world environments with ≤10⁴ states; no evaluation on continuous control, pixel-based observations, or deep RL settings where most modern RL applications exist, limiting impact for ICML

Strong practical assumptions limit applicability: Expected HSR (eHSR) requires solving pre-training tasks to optimality and having a task distribution; this two-stage offline construction is not always feasible, and practical comparison with online HSR costs is missing

Modest theoretical novelty: Combining SR with options is a straightforward extension; Theorem 3.1 (contraction property) follows naturally from τ≥1 and adds limited insight beyond existence of fixed point; no analysis of how temporal abstraction affects value approximation or transfer performance

Incomplete NMF analysis: The piecewise-smoothness intuition (p.4) lacks rigor; no formal characterization of when NMF recovers ground-truth parts or why it fails catastrophically on standard SR beyond qualitative 'feature collapse' argument; Figure 4d shows HSR-NMF matches SR-SVD reconstruction efficiency despite heavier spectral tail, unexplained

Online option discovery is heuristic: Appendix B.2 explicitly admits the procedure is 'deliberately simple and heuristic'; update frequency and sensitivity not discussed; acknowledged as future work, undermining claims of option-discovery independence

Incomplete comparison with related work: SR-GPI comparison (Figure 5) shows HSR-NMF only matches (not exceeds) SR-GPI with HSR features; limited discussion of recent transfer learning methods (bisimulation, contrastive learning); other hierarchical RL approaches not compared

Transfer efficiency metric lacks clarity: Defined ratio (p.6) conflates two effects; small absolute differences in Figure 2c (e.g., ~5-10 episodes) merit effect size reporting; alternative direct measures of transfer cost would be more interpretable
Critical edge case in Theorem 3.1: Contraction proof assumes τ_s^ā ≥ 1 for all options; behavior when options can terminate in 0 steps not addressed, potentially affecting theoretical guarantees

Missing key ablations: No sensitivity analysis for discount factor γ, different termination functions, or systematic failure cases; performance with poor options (e.g., covering options, Figure S4b) degrades significantly but not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear articulation of standard SR limitations (policy dependence, spectral diffusion)
Sound theoretical framework with rigorous proof of HSR Bellman operator contraction (Theorem 3.1)
Thorough experimental evaluation within scope: multiple topologies, option classes, proper statistical testing, good ablations (Figures S3-S4)
Insightful observation that HSR's piecewise-smooth geometry suits NMF better than SVD, with clear geometric intuition
Strong interpretability: HSR-NMF bases naturally align with topological features (bottlenecks), providing task-agnostic representations
Detailed reproducibility support: complete pseudocode (Algorithms S1-S3), implementation details, promised code availability
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: all experiments restricted to small discrete grid-worlds (max 50×50); claims about 'scaling to large procedurally generated environments' are misleading; no continuous control, visual observations, or deep RL—severely undermines practical relevance for 2026 venue
Artificially restrictive transfer setting: only reward changes in fixed transition dynamics; not true transfer learning; fails to test environmental changes that are essential for real-world transfer

Strong assumptions insufficiently analyzed: (1) requires good pre-defined options or admits heuristic online construction without principled algorithm, (2) eHSR requires pre-training distribution not validated for distribution shift, (3) no systematic analysis of option quality impact

Limited novelty: straightforward combination of three existing concepts (options + SR + NMF); key insight (NMF suits piecewise-smooth geometry) is observational rather than fundamental; lacks theoretical depth on why HSR achieves policy-robustness

Weak experimental baselines: Q-learning with linear function approximation is outdated; no comparison with modern representation learning (bisimulation, contrastive learning, recent hierarchical RL); 'Raw' baseline too weak to validate HSR contributions

Reproducibility gaps despite claims: NMF hyperparameter choices not specified (K=N defeats dimensionality reduction claims); sensitivity to K, convergence criteria, γ, learning rate α not analyzed; K=N experiments use full rank

Incomplete related work positioning: limited engagement with Successor Features literature; brief treatment of GPI (Section 4.3); exploration experiments (Section 4.4) only compare against SR, not state-of-the-art exploration methods

Restrictive assumptions undermine key claims: online option construction is 'largely heuristic' (p.6,9) with ad-hoc design; eHSR requirement for pre-training tasks partially contradicts policy-agnosticism claim; no failure mode analysis

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation addressing concrete limitations of classical SR (policy dependence and spectral diffusion) with compelling visual evidence
Sound technical approach with proper derivations, correct Bellman operator formulation (Eq. 4), and valid contraction proof (Theorem 3.1)
Novel insight about NMF suitability for HSR: well-demonstrated that HSR's piecewise-smooth structure enables effective sparse decomposition while standard SR suffers from topological feature collapse
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper statistical testing, multiple ablations across option types and environment topologies, and clear transfer efficiency metrics
Generality within scope: works with both pre-constructed and online options, robust across different grid-world topologies, benefits extend to exploration
Excellent presentation with clear writing, highly informative visualizations (Figure 1), detailed appendices with pseudocode and implementation details
Strong empirical results demonstrating robustness to policy changes, with quantitative evidence (Figure 2g) that HSR matrices change less than SR matrices following policy adaptation
weaknesses: Exclusively limited to discrete grid-world environments - a significant limitation for 2026 ICML standards that makes practical applicability to modern deep RL (images, continuous states) unclear and limits the scope of transferability claims

Dependence on effective option discovery: strongest results require pre-constructed eigenoptions from random-walk SR; online option construction is acknowledged as 'deliberately simple and heuristic' and shows substantially diminished benefits, undermining practical utility in new domains

Narrow transfer scenarios: evaluations are mostly 'same environment, different reward' transfers; no evaluation on significantly different topologies or truly diverse task families, making 'robust transfer' claims stronger than evidence warrants

Limited theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1's contraction proof follows straightforwardly from SR results; no formal analysis of why temporal abstraction improves transfer or sample complexity bounds
Modest conceptual novelty - combining well-established techniques (options, NMF, SR) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas, though the combination is empirically validated
'Policy-agnostic' claims need qualification: HSR depends on high-level policy μ in Eq. 4; eHSR only mitigates this with pre-training; stability claims are relative to SR, not absolute
NMF theoretical analysis incomplete: 'feature collapse' explanation is empirical; lacks formal characterization of conditions under which piecewise-smoothness enables NMF success

Limited baseline comparisons: no empirical evaluation against other modern representation learning methods (bisimulation, contrastive learning); SR-GPI comparison conflates orthogonal approaches (policy composition vs. representation learning)
Exploration results (Section 4.4) feel somewhat disconnected from main transfer narrative and diminish substantially with online options, reducing practical relevance
Missing analysis of when HSR underperforms or is inappropriate; inadequate investigation of failure modes (e.g., why covering options perform poorly)
